notes: Monday 23 Nov 2026 world issue (Taipei ~08:00). Window: Fri 20 – Sun 22 Nov (US/Europe). Economy: Wall Street worst week since 2020 as Anthropic IPO lands; UK offshore wealth tops £1tn; polar vortex threatens Europe gas; court bans BYD Defender clone in EU. Tech: Trump threatens ban on overseas AI data centres; Claude-assisted Riemann hypothesis proof verified; DNI warns of more outages; Google workers back AI-free school search. Politics: Democrats win biggest House majority since 1992; COP31 collapses; Russian warship sunk in Benghazi; Trump order on contractors and Congress. Literature (US): Jonathan Yardley dies; NBA writers on writer's block; best-reviewed books; Steven Thrasher on ICE at an LA ER. Society: Lebanese families return to wrecked homes; Virginia measles death; Korean minister quits over AI exam cheating; Indonesia factory fire.

stories.headline: Wall Street's worst week since 2020: Nvidia sinks 23%, even as Anthropic's record IPO lands
stories.dek: The Nasdaq fell 10% in five days. Anthropic raised a record $93.5 billion but ended the week worth about $1.6 trillion.
stories.caveman: Last week was a split-screen on Wall Street. On one side, Anthropic, the company behind the Claude chatbot, held the biggest stock market launch ever: it raised a record $93.5 billion, plus $26 billion more from big tech companies. Its shares rose 17% on day one. On the other side, the wider market had a terrible week. The Nasdaq, home of many tech stocks, dropped 10%, its worst week since the start of Covid in 2020. Nvidia, the top AI chip maker, fell 23%, its sharpest weekly drop in 18 years, as it deals with the scandal around its former CEO. Investors are worried about rising interest rates, growing public anger at AI, and whether all the money poured into AI will pay off. By Friday, Anthropic was valued at about $1.6 trillion.
stories.why_it_matters: When US tech stocks crash, Taiwan's stock market usually follows, because Taiwan makes most of the world's AI chips. This is a big reason Taiwan's market had its worst week ever.
stories.camps: Optimists say the Anthropic IPO proves there is still huge demand for AI, and the sell-off is a healthy cooling. Pessimists see signs of a bubble: very high prices, falling chip stocks, and doubts that AI companies can earn enough to justify their value.
stories.image_alt: Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei at the Nasdaq MarketSite before the company's trading debut
stories.image_credit: Photo: AFP via Getty Images / CNBC

terms.explain: Initial public offering: the first time a private company sells shares to the public.
A big US stock market where many tech companies are listed; also the name of its main index.
What the whole company is worth, based on its share price.

stories.headline: UK savers now hold more than £1 trillion in tax havens
stories.dek: Money in offshore accounts grew 10% in two years; the tax office struggles to track some of it.
stories.caveman: A tax haven is a place with very low taxes and lots of secrecy, like the British Virgin Islands, Jersey, Switzerland or Panama. New data from Britain's tax office (HMRC), obtained by the TaxWatch think tank, shows that people who pay tax in the UK now keep more than £1 trillion in accounts in these places, the first time it has passed that mark. The amount grew 10% between 2022 and 2024. Keeping money offshore is not illegal if you declare it. But some of it is hard to trace. The tax office recovers about £125 million a year in unpaid tax from offshore accounts, but it once estimated £200 million to £700 million goes unpaid each year. About one in five accounts reported to the UK by other countries had no taxpayer ID number, which makes matching them to real people hard.
stories.why_it_matters: When rich people hide money, governments collect less tax and ordinary workers carry more of the load. Many countries, including Taiwan, face the same problem.
stories.camps: Campaigners say governments should force banks to collect proper ID and close loopholes. Others point out most offshore money is declared legally, and that people use these accounts for business or because they live abroad.
stories.image_alt: Road Town, capital of the British Virgin Islands, a major offshore financial centre
stories.image_credit: Photo: Todd VanSickle/AP via The Guardian

terms.explain: A country or territory with very low taxes and secret banking, where people park money.
HM Revenue and Customs, the UK government department that collects taxes.
A bank account in a different country from where you live or pay tax.

stories.headline: A record-early polar vortex breakdown could mean a cold winter and pricey gas for Europe
stories.dek: Europe started winter with its lowest gas storage in more than a decade, and Middle East supplies are disrupted.
stories.caveman: High above the North Pole, strong winds usually spin in a circle and keep the very cold air trapped there. This is called the polar vortex. Weather experts say it is breaking down earlier than ever recorded this year. When that happens, freezing air can spill south into Europe and North America. At the same time, there is an unusually strong El Niño, a warming of the Pacific Ocean that shakes up weather around the world. Together, they raise the risk of a long cold spell. That worries energy traders: Europe began this winter with the lowest gas stored in more than ten years. If people need lots of heating, Europe will have to buy more liquefied gas shipped from abroad, just as supplies from the Middle East are disrupted. That could push prices up.
stories.why_it_matters: Gas is a global market. If Europe scrambles for gas, prices can rise for Asian buyers too, including Taiwan, which imports almost all its energy.
stories.camps: Some scientists say an early breakdown does not guarantee a harsh winter; weather is hard to predict months ahead. Traders say even the risk is enough to make prices jumpy.
stories.image_alt: NOAA satellite image of a low-pressure system from the polar vortex over the northern US (2014)
stories.image_credit: Image: NOAA via Getty Images / CNBC

terms.explain: A big ring of strong winds high above the North Pole that keeps freezing air in the Arctic.
A natural warming of the Pacific Ocean that changes weather around the world.
Liquefied natural gas: gas cooled into a liquid so it can be shipped on boats.

stories.headline: Court bans China's BYD from selling its 'Defender clone' SUV in the EU
stories.dek: A Dutch judge said BYD's Ti7 copies the look of Jaguar Land Rover's Defender.
stories.caveman: BYD is a giant Chinese car company. One of its SUVs, the Ti7, looks a lot like the famous British Land Rover Defender, so much that car magazines nicknamed it the 'Chinese Defender clone'. Jaguar Land Rover (JLR) took BYD to court. A judge in The Hague, in the Netherlands, ruled that the Ti7 breaks JLR's protected European design rights, so BYD cannot sell it in the EU. The ban starts one week after Friday's ruling. BYD said it had no concrete plans to sell the car in the EU anyway. But the court said it had no power over the UK, where the Ti7 is on sale for £47,995, more than £20,000 cheaper than a Defender, with deliveries due from January.
stories.why_it_matters: Chinese carmakers are growing fast in Europe. Cases like this test how far 'inspired by' can go before it becomes copying.
stories.camps: JLR and many European makers say design is valuable work that must be protected. BYD's fans say cars in the same category naturally look similar, and that cheaper choices are good for buyers.
stories.image_alt: The BYD Fangchengbao 7, known as the Ti7 in some markets, at the Beijing Auto Show
stories.image_credit: Photo: Adek Berry/AFP/Getty Images via The Guardian

terms.explain: Legal ownership of ideas and designs, like patents, trademarks and design rights.
A legal protection for how a product looks.
Sport utility vehicle: a big, tall car often built for rough roads.

stories.headline: Trump threatens to ban US tech firms from building AI data centres abroad
stories.dek: He promised a 'tremendous tax' on companies that do it, saying 'China will take all of them'. Details are thin.
stories.caveman: A data centre is a huge warehouse full of computers that run AI apps like ChatGPT and Claude. US companies such as Meta and Google have deals to build some in other countries. President Trump said he will not allow American companies to build data centres outside the US, and that those who do would face a 'tremendous tax'. His reason: 'China will take all of them.' He admitted his own team was hearing the idea for the first time. It is unclear how such a rule would work. Data centres were a big issue in this month's US midterm elections: many people near them complain about noise and huge electricity use, and many winning Democrats promised tougher rules. Earlier in the week, the US also said firms will need a licence to buy advanced chips, so officials can check they are not helping Chinese companies.
stories.why_it_matters: Taiwan makes most of the chips that go into these data centres. Where they are built, and who may buy chips, affects Taiwan's biggest industry.
stories.camps: Supporters say keeping AI infrastructure at home protects US security and jobs. Critics say it would hurt US companies abroad, upset allies, and is hard to enforce. Local communities in the US are split on whether they want data centres at all.

terms.explain: A big building full of computers that store data and run online and AI services.
Government permission needed to sell certain goods to other countries.
US elections held halfway through a president's four-year term.

stories.headline: Experts verify claim that Anthropic's Claude helped prove the Riemann hypothesis, a 167-year-old maths puzzle
stories.dek: Two groups checked the proof; it is one of seven 'Millennium Prize' problems worth $1m each.
stories.caveman: The Riemann hypothesis is one of the most famous unsolved problems in maths. It is about prime numbers, numbers like 2, 3, 5 and 7 that can only be divided by 1 and themselves, and how they are spread along the number line. It was proposed in 1859, and a $1 million prize has been offered since 2000 for solving it. Levent Alpöge, a mathematician who works at Anthropic, posted a note on Friday saying the AI system Claude helped him build a proof over about six weeks. He shared it in Lean, a computer language that lets a machine check every step. On Saturday, two groups, the Lean Focused Research Organization and the Mathlib Initiative, said they had independently verified it. Alpöge admitted the timing, one day after Anthropic's stock market debut, was 'horrible'.
stories.why_it_matters: If confirmed by the wider maths world, this would be one of the biggest moments ever for AI: a machine helping crack a problem humans failed at for over a century.
stories.camps: Many celebrate a new way of doing science. But some mathematicians are uneasy about rich private companies driving discovery, and about trusting AI. An Italian mathematician who released his own incomplete proof the same day said he avoided AI because he does not fully trust it.
stories.image_alt: Anthropic employees at the Nasdaq during the company's market debut
stories.image_credit: Photo: Brendan McDermid/Reuters via The Guardian

terms.explain: A famous 1859 maths idea about how prime numbers are spread out; unproven until now.
A whole number bigger than 1 that can only be divided by 1 and itself.
A computer language for writing maths proofs so a computer can check every step.

stories.headline: US intelligence chief warns of more 'bumps in the road' after tech outages
stories.dek: Recent breakdowns hit flights, Microsoft Outlook and bank payments; officials say there is no sign of a cyberattack.
stories.caveman: In the past couple of weeks, several big tech systems in the US broke down: a nationwide stop on flights for hours, an outage of Microsoft's Outlook email, and slower bank payments. Many people feared hackers or AI attacks. Officials say no. The flight stop was caused by a router upgrade that flooded systems with data, and Microsoft said its problem came from a network upgrade. Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton told CNN that Americans should expect more 'bumps in the road' as companies and the government upgrade systems for the AI age, and should expect big spending on cybersecurity. His warning comes before Thanksgiving week, one of the busiest travel times of the year.
stories.why_it_matters: Modern life runs on a few giant systems. When one breaks, millions of people are stuck, no matter where they live.
stories.camps: Officials say outages during upgrades are normal and not sinister. Critics ask whether the government is downplaying the problems, noting that the White House recently removed its cybersecurity chief after the outages, which raises questions about who is in charge.
stories.image_alt: Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton testifying in Congress on 18 November

terms.explain: When a service or system stops working for a while.
A device that directs internet traffic between networks.
Protecting computers and networks from attacks and failures.

stories.headline: Hundreds of Google workers back parents who want AI-free search for schools
stories.dek: More than 550 employees signed a petition after Google said it won't separate AI from its education tools.
stories.caveman: When you search on Google now, an AI summary often appears at the top. Many parents and teachers want schools to be able to use Google Search without the AI part, so kids learn to find and judge information themselves. Google has said it will not unbundle AI from its tools for education. Last week, parents and educators protested outside Google offices in six cities. Now more than 550 Google employees have signed a petition asking the company to give schools an AI-free option, and the workers' union warns schools might drop Google products altogether. NPR reports that Google earlier won two court cases by arguing that AI Overviews and Search are one single tool, which may make splitting them legally awkward. Google did not comment. Some school districts are looking at workarounds such as browser extensions.
stories.why_it_matters: Students everywhere, including in Taiwan, use Google. How much AI sits between kids and real sources is a big question for education.
stories.camps: Parents and many teachers say children need to learn research skills before relying on AI. Google and AI supporters argue AI is part of modern life and students should learn to use it well. The legal angle shows companies' court arguments can lock in their choices.

terms.explain: The AI-written summary Google shows at the top of some search results.
A written request signed by many people asking for change.
To separate parts of a product so people can choose them one by one.

stories.headline: Democrats win their biggest House majority since 1992
stories.dek: With at least 258 of 435 seats, Democrats will control both chambers of Congress from January, facing a Republican president.
stories.caveman: The US Congress has two parts: the House of Representatives (435 seats) and the Senate. On Sunday, Democrat Chuck Hubbard beat long-time Republican Virginia Foxx in North Carolina after a recount, giving Democrats at least 258 House seats. That is their largest majority since 1992. Democrats gained 44 seats, more than the 40 they won in 2018. Four races are still not decided. Because Democrats also won the Senate, the country will have a divided government: Congress controlled by Democrats, the White House by Republican President Trump. Democrats are planning a 100-day agenda on the cost of living, and many investigations of the Trump administration. House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries says he is willing to work with Republicans on some issues.
stories.why_it_matters: Who controls Congress decides US laws, budgets and investigations, including policies on trade, chips and support for Taiwan.
stories.camps: Democrats call it a clear message from voters about prices and Trump's leadership. Republicans say midterms usually punish the president's party and that divided government will force compromise. Some voters worry it will mean two years of gridlock.
stories.image_alt: House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries at a news conference at the Capitol
stories.image_credit: Photo: Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images via The Guardian

terms.explain: The bigger chamber of the US Congress, with 435 members elected every two years.
Having more than half the seats, which lets a party control what gets voted on.
When one party controls Congress and the other holds the presidency.

stories.headline: COP31 climate talks collapse without a major deal
stories.dek: The final text did not even mention fossil fuels; the EU and Pacific island nations refused it. The last such collapse was in 2009.
stories.caveman: Every year, almost every country meets at a UN conference called a COP to agree how to fight climate change. This year's meeting, COP31 in Turkey, ran into Sunday, the longest ever, and still failed to produce a major new deal. The last draft did not mention 'fossil fuels' (coal, oil and gas), the main cause of global warming, even once. Earlier drafts did, but oil-producing countries objected. The EU, Pacific island countries, Panama and the Marshall Islands said the deal was far too weak. Saudi Arabia said Arab nations caused only a small part of past emissions, and Russia warned that moving off fossil fuels too fast would cause 'fuel poverty'. Poorer countries were also angry that rich countries made no clear promise of money to help them cope with heatwaves and droughts. UN chief Antonio Guterres said he was 'deeply disappointed'.
stories.why_it_matters: Climate change brings stronger typhoons, heat and sea-level rise, which threaten islands like Taiwan. When countries cannot agree, cutting emissions gets harder.
stories.camps: Climate-vulnerable countries and the EU say leaving out fossil fuels is unacceptable. Oil producers say they are being unfairly blamed and need time. Poorer countries say the real issue is money and fairness.
stories.image_alt: Delegates at the COP31 climate talks

terms.explain: Conference of the Parties: the yearly UN climate summit.
Coal, oil and gas: fuels that release carbon dioxide when burned.
Gases like carbon dioxide released into the air that heat up the planet.

stories.headline: Russian warship sinks in Libya after suspected Ukrainian sea-drone attack
stories.dek: The strike in Benghazi happened more than 1,000 miles from Ukraine, showing the war spreading far from the front.
stories.caveman: Early on Sunday, a Russian navy warship called the Merkury, docked in the port of Benghazi in Libya to refuel and load supplies, was hit and sank. Libyan officials said several Ukrainian sea drones (small unmanned boats packed with explosives) were launched at it; four were shot down and two hit the ship, causing a huge explosion. Satellite pictures showed the ship had sunk. Benghazi is on the Mediterranean, more than 1,000 miles from southern Ukraine. Hours later, a Russia-linked cargo ship said to be carrying military supplies was also hit by a sea drone off the same coast. Ukraine started the war with almost no navy but has used sea drones to push Russia's fleet away from much of the Black Sea.
stories.why_it_matters: It shows how cheap drones are changing war at sea, a lesson closely studied by Taiwan, which is also an island that depends on sea lanes.
stories.camps: Ukraine and its supporters see it as a smart way to hit Russia's war machine far from home. Others worry the war is spilling into new regions such as North Africa, raising the risk for countries that host Russian ships.
stories.image_alt: Satellite image of the capsized Russian corvette Merkury in Benghazi

terms.explain: A small unmanned boat, often carrying explosives, steered from far away.
A small, fast warship.
A port city in eastern Libya, on the Mediterranean Sea.

stories.headline: Trump orders federal contractors to check with the White House before answering Congress
stories.dek: Companies that refuse could lose their government contracts, as Democrats prepare investigations from January.
stories.caveman: Many private companies get paid by the US government to build things or provide services. They are called federal contractors. A new executive order signed late Friday by President Trump tells these companies to consult the White House about any questions they get from Congress, to coordinate their answers, and to hold back communications the White House sees as 'privileged' (private). If they do not, their contracts could be cancelled. Democrats, who take control of Congress in January, have said government contracts, especially money flowing to companies linked to Trump's family, will be a top target of their investigations. The White House has already told federal agencies they need approval before appearing before Congress.
stories.why_it_matters: In a democracy, Congress is supposed to check the president's power. This order is about who gets to see information, a basic civics question about checks and balances.
stories.camps: The White House says it is protecting confidential executive-branch information. Critics, including many legal experts and Democrats, say it is an attempt to block oversight and scare companies into silence. Courts may end up deciding where the line is.
stories.image_alt: Donald Trump at the White House on 5 November
stories.image_credit: Photo: Elizabeth Frantz/Reuters via The Guardian

terms.explain: A written instruction from the US president that tells government agencies what to do.
Congress checking and investigating what the government is doing.
A private company paid by the US government to do work.

stories.headline: Remembered: Jonathan Yardley, the critic who 'pulled zero punches'
stories.dek: The Pulitzer-winning Washington Post book critic reviewed about 3,000 books. He died at 87.
stories.caveman: Jonathan Yardley was one of America's best-known book critics. He wrote reviews for The Washington Post for 33 years, about 3,000 of them, after winning a Pulitzer Prize for criticism in 1981. He died on Friday in Washington at 87, his son confirmed. Yardley was famous for being blunt. He said attacking a bad book was more fun to write than praising a good one, because 'wonderful' and 'extraordinary' get boring. But his praise could make careers: he helped champion John Kennedy Toole, Anne Tyler, Michael Chabon and Edward P. Jones. From 2003 he wrote 'Second Reading', a column bringing back forgotten books. He believed a critic who only wrote nice reviews had no credibility.
stories.why_it_matters: Book critics act like guides in a huge library. Yardley's death is a reminder of the era when one newspaper critic could make or break a book.
stories.camps: Fans remember him as honest and fearless, saving readers time and money. Some authors he attacked felt he could be harsh or unfair. Both sides agree he took books seriously.

terms.explain: A person whose job is to judge and review books, films, art or music.
Top US award for journalism, books and music.
A news article about someone who has recently died and their life.

stories.headline: Hot: how National Book Award writers beat writer's block
stories.dek: Edwidge Danticat ignores it, Sara Nović writes by hand, and Fady Joudah calls it a kind of meditation.
stories.caveman: The National Book Awards are among America's top book prizes, and the winners were just announced. Literary Hub asked finalists and winners how they deal with writer's block, when words just won't come. Edwidge Danticat (Dèy) says she simply refuses to accept it: if a piece isn't coming, it isn't ready yet, so she reads or writes shorter things. Morgan Thomas (Mad Eden) says not wanting to write is often a sign to rest, take walks or spend time with family, but around 75% through a book she has to push on anyway. Sara Nović (Mother Tongue) goes back to pen and notebook, because a blank page forces new words. Poet Fady Joudah (Exhibit G, about Gaza) says he doesn't call it a 'block' at all, but a silence that rewards him later.
stories.why_it_matters: Anyone who writes, from students to office workers, gets stuck. Great writers' small habits can help everyone.
stories.camps: Some writers say discipline is everything: sit down and write. Others say rest and living life are part of the work. The answers show there is no single right way.

terms.explain: When a writer feels stuck and cannot produce new writing.
Major yearly US book prizes for fiction, nonfiction, poetry, translation and young people's literature.
One of the last few people still in the running for a prize.

stories.headline: Hot: critics' favourite books this week, from Nick Harkaway's Le Carré sequel to Shteyngart on pleasure
stories.dek: Lit Hub's Book Marks tally of reviews puts The Taper Man and Hermione Lee's Anita Brookner biography on top.
stories.caveman: Book Marks, a site from Literary Hub, collects reviews from many newspapers and magazines and counts how many are raves, positive, mixed or pans. This week's top fiction is The Taper Man by Nick Harkaway, a new novel set in the spy world of his late father John le Carré; one reviewer says 'George Smiley is in good hands.' Also high: Uprising by Tahmima Anam, Nanny Nanny by K Chiucarello, The Runner by Scarlett Thomas, and Amazons by 'Cleo Birdwell', a playful old novel tied to Don DeLillo. In nonfiction, Hermione Lee's biography Anita Brookner: Art and Life got 12 raves; also listed are Gerald Martin's life of Mario Vargas Llosa and Gary Shteyngart's The Sensualist: Adventures in Pure Pleasure.
stories.why_it_matters: These lists show which books US critics are excited about right now, a quick shortcut for what to read next.
stories.camps: Review roundups help readers, but critics often favour big publishers and famous names. Smaller books can get missed, so many readers mix lists like this with word of mouth and indie bookstores.
stories.image_alt: Cover art for Gary Shteyngart's The Sensualist

terms.explain: A very enthusiastic review.
A very negative review.
A book about someone's life written by another person.

stories.headline: Hot topic: writer Steven Thrasher on ICE agents blocking an LA emergency room
stories.dek: In a Lit Hub essay, the author of The Viral Underclass asks what happens to health when people fear hospitals.
stories.caveman: US writers are using essays to respond to immigration raids. In Literary Hub, author and journalist Steven W. Thrasher writes about 7 November, when ICE (US immigration agents) brought a detained man to a hospital emergency room in Boyle Heights, a mostly Latino neighbourhood of Los Angeles. The hospital says agents formed a line across its ambulance entrance, so it sent ambulances to other hospitals for about two hours. The hospital says it does not take part in immigration enforcement. Activists gathered, and at least two protesters, both US citizens, were detained, according to a local rights network. Thrasher argues the real damage is fear: people may skip medical care because they are afraid. He notes ICE, the hospital and activists dispute many details.
stories.why_it_matters: Literature is not only novels. Essays like this shape how readers understand news, and show writers taking sides on public issues.
stories.camps: Supporters of strict immigration enforcement say agents must be able to do their jobs, including at hospitals. Health workers and immigrant-rights groups say hospitals must stay safe places for everyone, or public health suffers.

terms.explain: US Immigration and Customs Enforcement, the agency that arrests and deports immigrants.
A short piece of nonfiction writing that argues a point or reflects on a topic.
The hospital department for urgent, sudden illness or injury.

stories.headline: Lebanese families return to burned and wrecked homes as Israeli troops pull back
stories.dek: In one southern village, a couple found their house occupied, then set on fire; their son, a volunteer medic, was killed in March.
stories.caveman: Southern Lebanon sits next to Israel. Israel has fought there against Hezbollah, an armed group backed by Iran. Under a US-brokered plan, Israeli troops are leaving some villages and the Lebanese army is taking over. NPR visited Zawtar al-Gharbiyah, the first village in this test. Atef Kadouh and Soumaya Yaghi had lived in their house for 40 years. When they came back, they found Israeli soldiers had used it, and it was set on fire as they left: bullet holes in the fridge, smashed furniture, a burned grandchild's bedroom. Their youngest son Adel, a sports teacher who became a volunteer ambulance driver, was killed with four other medics in an Israeli drone strike in March while burying an elderly man. Lebanon's Health Ministry says Israel has killed more than 135 first responders in two years. Israel's military says, without giving proof, that militants pose as medics.
stories.why_it_matters: War does not end when the shooting stops. Families must rebuild homes and lives, and rules that protect medics matter everywhere.
stories.camps: Israel says it acts against real threats to its northern towns and has destroyed homes in a 'security zone'. Lebanese families and rights groups say homes and medics are being targeted unfairly and want accountability.
stories.image_alt: A destroyed home in Zawtar al-Gharbiyah, southern Lebanon

terms.explain: An armed group and political party in Lebanon, backed by Iran.
Medics, firefighters and others who rush to help in emergencies.
An agreement to stop fighting.

stories.headline: A young child dies of measles in Virginia as the US outbreak worsens
stories.dek: The US recently lost its 'measles eliminated' status after 26 years; Pennsylvania has reported eight deaths.
stories.caveman: Measles is a very contagious disease that a vaccine can prevent. Virginia reported its first measles-linked death of 2026 on Friday: a child aged four or younger. The state did not say if the child was vaccinated. Virginia has had 220 cases this year, and 179 of them were in unvaccinated people. Pennsylvania, the hardest-hit state, has reported eight measles deaths and 1,631 cases; Wisconsin has reported two deaths and New York one. The US recently lost its 'measles elimination' status, which it had held for 26 years. State and federal death counts don't match, because the CDC under Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. started using a different data source. Health experts say trusted local messengers are key to reaching communities, such as the Amish, where outbreaks spread.
stories.why_it_matters: Measles can kill children and spreads across borders through travel. Taiwan keeps high vaccine rates to stay protected.
stories.camps: Doctors and public health experts say vaccines are safe and the best protection. Some parents distrust vaccines or government health officials, and critics say mixed messages from the top of US health policy have made things worse.
stories.image_alt: A measles clinic in Andrews, Texas, in 2025
stories.image_credit: Photo: Annie Rice/AP via The Guardian

terms.explain: A very contagious virus that causes fever and rash and can be deadly for kids.
When a country has no ongoing spread of a disease for at least a year.
The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, the national public health agency.

stories.headline: South Korea's education minister quits over AI exam-cheating panic
stories.dek: Phones across the country blared emergency alerts during the national college exam; 111 students were caught with devices.
stories.caveman: In South Korea, one exam called the Suneung decides which university many students get into, and it shapes careers. About 500,000 students took it on Thursday. A week before, the top scorer of a national tax accountant exam admitted he cheated: he used a tiny camera to photograph questions, sent them to an AI, and read answers on his phone. Officials panicked and rushed out new rules. During the Suneung, they sent three national emergency alerts that made phones across the country blare, even on silent and even tourists' phones, to expose hidden devices. Students had to cover shirt buttons that might hide cameras. Officials found 111 students with unauthorised smart devices. Education Minister Choi Kyo-jin resigned, saying he took responsibility for the confusion, and President Lee Jae Myung accepted.
stories.why_it_matters: AI makes cheating easier everywhere. Taiwan's schools and exams face the same question of how to keep tests fair without treating everyone like a suspect.
stories.camps: Some praised strict action to protect fairness in a high-stakes exam. Others said last-minute measures like nationwide alarms were chaotic and overkill. Many, including the president, say the deeper problem is an exam system that puts so much pressure on one day.
stories.image_alt: South Korean high school students check their answers a day after the college entrance exam

terms.explain: South Korea's national college entrance exam, taken once a year.
A loud government message sent to every phone in an area.
To quit a job, often to take responsibility for a problem.

stories.headline: Fire at Indonesian sweets factory kills at least three; dozens of workers missing
stories.dek: About 60 people were believed inside; rescuers recovered 24 body bags as the search went on.
stories.caveman: On Saturday evening a fire broke out at a confectionery (sweets) factory in Serang, Banten province, about 50 km west of Jakarta, Indonesia's capital. When firefighters arrived, a large area was already burning. Officials confirmed at least three deaths and said about 36 people were missing, many believed trapped inside. About 60 people were thought to be in the building. Rescuers found 15 survivors, and four people were treated for injuries. By Sunday evening, they had recovered 24 body bags, so the death toll is expected to rise. Relatives waited outside for news. The cause is not yet known. The factory belongs to PT Fonusa Agung Mulia, which describes itself as part of UNIFAM, one of Indonesia's largest food companies.
stories.why_it_matters: Factory fires often show weak safety rules for workers. Many products sold around Asia, including in Taiwan, come from factories like this.
stories.camps: Officials say they are focused on rescue and finding the cause. Workers' groups usually ask whether exits, alarms and fire systems were working, and who will be held responsible.
